rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that the holiday would increase turnout through civic engagement even if some scheduling barriers remain.
rebuttals.objection: Higher motivation or perceived civic value cannot be relied on to produce higher turnout when the underlying work-time constraints still prevent people from taking time to vote.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that the holiday would be justified because it elevates civic participation and democracy.
rebuttals.objection: If the holiday does not reliably remove the main barriers for low-income workers, then the civic-importance argument does not make it an effective turnout policy.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that the holiday would meaningfully improve access to voting by easing schedule conflicts.
rebuttals.objection: A holiday leaves voter-registration hurdles in place, because it does not automatically register eligible voters or change registration rules, so it cannot by itself provide comprehensive voting access.

rebuttals.target: AG1's assumption that a holiday plus some schedule relief is enough to materially raise turnout.
rebuttals.objection: Even if a holiday helps some people with time off, unresolved registration barriers will still stop some eligible voters, so turnout gains cannot be substantial on that basis alone.

rebuttals.target: AG1's proposal that a holiday is preferable to targeted reforms.
rebuttals.objection: Targeted reforms such as employer time-off requirements and automatic voter registration directly address the key barriers to voting and are therefore better than relying on a federal holiday.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that the holiday is worse than targeted reforms because it does not solve voting access comprehensively.
rebuttals.objection: A national holiday can be implemented alongside other voting-access reforms rather than replacing them, so it is not inherently worse just because it is not a complete solution by itself.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that the holiday does not reliably produce meaningful turnout gains.
rebuttals.objection: A holiday can still produce real voting-access gains by removing a major barrier, even if it does not solve every voting obstacle at once.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that the holiday's turnout logic is invalid because it does not guarantee comprehensive access.
rebuttals.objection: The holiday can work as a complement to other reforms, combining practical access gains with civic symbolism, so it should not be rejected merely because it is not a substitute for every other reform.

rebuttals.target: AG1's argument that civic motivation and celebration will boost turnout.
rebuttals.objection: For many low-income workers, private retail and service employers can remain open and keep regular shifts on federal holidays, so the holiday does not reliably remove the work constraints that determine whether they can vote.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that increased motivation and civic value will translate into turnout.
rebuttals.objection: If practical work-time constraints remain, then motivation alone cannot be expected to overcome the inability to take time off to vote.

rebuttals.target: AG1's overall turnout rationale for a holiday.
rebuttals.objection: An Election Day holiday by itself is unlikely to produce meaningful turnout gains because it does not reliably solve the problems faced by low-income private-employer workers.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday would be a good reform because it combines motivation with access.
rebuttals.objection: Making Election Day a federal holiday disadvantages low-income workers because private employers are not required to provide paid time off, so workers may still have to work or lose wages to vote.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday meaningfully improves the ability to find time to vote.
rebuttals.objection: A federal holiday does not automatically register voters or fix registration requirements, so people blocked by registration problems still cannot vote even if schedules improve.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that easing schedules and boosting motivation together can reliably convert people into voters.
rebuttals.objection: If a voter is not registered or still faces registration hurdles, then better scheduling or higher motivation does not make that person able to cast a ballot.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that the holiday can add turnout gains on top of other reforms.
rebuttals.objection: The holiday is still not sufficient by itself to overcome major voting barriers, so targeted reforms remain the more reliable approach.

rebuttals.target: AG1's bottom-line proposal that Election Day should be a national holiday.
rebuttals.objection: Election Day should not be a national holiday because it leaves key work constraints in place for many low-income workers while also failing to address registration barriers.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reduce school/work scheduling barriers for millions, especially low-income workers
rebuttals.objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to give paid time off, so many low-income retail and service workers could still be scheduled to work and would not reliably get time to vote.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would increase participation by removing scheduling barriers
rebuttals.objection: If low-income workers still have to work on Election Day, the main work-related barriers remain, so the holiday would leave those workers disadvantaged rather than broadly improving access.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would meaningfully boost turnout
rebuttals.objection: Research suggests that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that foreign precedent shows the holiday is feasible and workable
rebuttals.objection: State laws requiring employer time off to vote and automatic voter registration are more reliable ways to reduce voting barriers than relying on a holiday.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s objection that a federal holiday would still leave many low-income workers working and thus not help them
rebuttals.objection: School closures on federal holidays also remove childcare and school-day scheduling conflicts, which can be a major barrier for parents and caregivers, including low-income families.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would disadvantage low-income workers
rebuttals.objection: Low-income families often rely on predictable school schedules and have fewer childcare alternatives, so reducing school and childcare conflicts can actually improve their ability to vote even if some workplaces remain open.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s implication that only complete removal of every work barrier would count as a useful reform
rebuttals.objection: A holiday need not eliminate every barrier for every voter to be worthwhile; if it meaningfully reduces barriers for millions, that is enough to justify it.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s claim that private employers are not required to give paid time off on a federal holiday, so a holiday would not reduce work barriers
rebuttals.objection: Even without a legal paid-leave mandate, many employers reduce hours or close on federal holidays, so a holiday would often create real time away from work for at least some hourly workers.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not reliably solve work-related voting barriers
rebuttals.objection: If a holiday reduces the number of people who must remain on shift during Election Day, it still reduces work-related voting barriers for millions of Americans, including many low-income hourly workers.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s argument that a holiday does not increase participation because it does not guarantee paid leave
rebuttals.objection: The proposal is about reducing voting time constraints and making voting easier to fit into people’s schedules; even partial reductions in those constraints can increase participation.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that school-day timing and childcare conflicts make a holiday helpful
rebuttals.objection: The relevant question is whether the holiday reliably removes the barriers that matter most; school closures may help some parents, but they do not address the core work-schedule problem for low-income hourly workers.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that school closures and a celebratory framing make the holiday broadly beneficial
rebuttals.objection: Because a federal holiday is not the same as a mandated paid day off, the policy’s effect depends on voluntary employer behavior rather than a legal guarantee, so it can preserve or worsen income-based access gaps.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that school/childcare scheduling conflicts mean a holiday would improve access for low-income families
rebuttals.objection: If a policy does not reliably provide voting time to the least flexible workers, it risks leaving unequal voting access in place rather than fixing it.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s reliance on OECD countries that hold elections on weekends or holidays as evidence the idea works
rebuttals.objection: Other countries’ election-day holidays do not show that a U.S. federal holiday would work the same way, because U.S. private employers are not required to give paid time off under federal holiday law.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that cross-party support and foreign precedent show the policy is workable
rebuttals.objection: The fact that many people support the idea does not answer whether it actually solves the problem; a popular policy can still be ineffective at increasing turnout.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not reliably give low-income workers time to vote
rebuttals.objection: The proposal is aimed at reducing voting barriers broadly, not guaranteeing perfect paid leave for every worker; the absence of a perfect guarantee does not by itself show the holiday should be rejected.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s claim that foreign precedent does not help because U.S. holiday law differs
rebuttals.objection: OECD countries show that elections on weekends or holidays are compatible with functioning democracies, so the foreign precedent still supports the feasibility of the approach.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s claim that turnout research defeats the holiday proposal
rebuttals.objection: Even if the holiday is not the single most effective turnout reform, it can still be justified if it reduces scheduling barriers and elevates the civic meaning of voting.

rebuttals.target: Agent 1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reduce scheduling barriers for many voters, especially low-income workers
rebuttals.objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, and many low-income workers in retail and service jobs would still be scheduled to work, so the holiday would not reliably remove their voting-time barriers.

rebuttals.target: Agent 1’s assumption that a national holiday would broadly solve time-off problems for low-income voters
rebuttals.objection: Because the holiday would not reliably eliminate the main work-schedule barrier for low-income workers, it would disadvantage them by leaving the core obstacle in place rather than fixing it.

rebuttals.target: Agent 1’s preference for a national holiday over other reforms
rebuttals.objection: State laws requiring employers to give time off to vote, or automatic voter registration, are more reliable ways to remove voting barriers because they directly address the relevant obstacle instead of depending on private employers’ holiday practices.

rebuttals.target: Agent 2’s claim that a federal Election Day holiday would not change retail and service staffing enough to help workers vote
rebuttals.objection: Even though federal holidays do not force private employers to close, they usually influence scheduling, holiday staffing, reduced hours, or shift flexibility, so retail and service workplaces would likely make some schedule adjustments that help workers vote.

rebuttals.target: Agent 2’s broader assumption that retail and service employers would keep Election Day staffing essentially unchanged
rebuttals.objection: There is no basis for assuming retail and service employers would universally keep the same staffing patterns despite a federal holiday; holiday status commonly affects work schedules in practice.

rebuttals.target: Agent 2’s claim that the holiday would not meaningfully help low-income workers
rebuttals.objection: Because holiday-style scheduling can create reduced hours, shift swaps, or more flexibility, low-income retail and service workers would be more likely to have time to vote, so the holiday would still reduce scheduling barriers for them.

rebuttals.target: Agent 2’s claim that the holiday would not help low-income voters because their main problem is employer schedules
rebuttals.objection: The scheduling barriers at issue include school-related demands as well as work schedules, so even low-income voters can benefit from the school-day relief created by a national holiday.

rebuttals.target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday by itself would not reliably or meaningfully increase turnout
rebuttals.objection: A national holiday would reduce both work and school scheduling barriers and would also frame voting as a civic celebration, so it would reliably and meaningfully increase turnout rather than fail to do so.

rebuttals.target: Agent 2’s claim that low-income workers would still face the main time-off constraint on Election Day despite the holiday
rebuttals.objection: Because many eligible voters are blocked primarily by day-of scheduling conflicts, and a holiday gives time off from work and school, the holiday would remove a major barrier even if some private employers still schedule some workers.

rebuttals.target: Agent 2’s claim that remaining administrative or eligibility barriers prevent a holiday from meaningfully increasing turnout
rebuttals.objection: The existence of other barriers does not negate the impact of removing major work/school time-off barriers, so a holiday can still produce meaningful turnout gains for voters whose main obstacle is scheduling.
